title: Optional Mathematics: Unit-wise Objective Question Bank

toc.title: 17.4 Trigonometry: Multiple, Submultiple and Transformation Formulas
17.5 Conditional Identities, Trigonometric Equations and Height and Distance
17.6 Angle between Two Lines and Pair of Straight Lines

html:
Optional Mathematics is the paper where a single mark costs the least work and the most care. Group A of the SEE paper carries ten one-mark items and the first item of almost every later group is also a one-line recall, so roughly a quarter of the paper can be won or lost on formulas that take ten seconds each. This chapter drills those items unit by unit, in multiple-choice form, so that every answer can be checked instantly and every mistake has a name.

Each section opens with a facts line — the four to six results that the items in that section actually use — then gives items, then gives a key with a one-line reason. Work an item in under a minute; correct it in ten seconds; move on.

The shape of the paper (CDC grid, 2082)
Group Items Marks each Total What it tests
A 10 1 10 direct recall, single step
B 8 2 16 one short method
C 11 3 33 a full short-answer method
D 4 4 16 longer method, proof or construction
Total 33 75 3 hours

Group A is 13% of the paper but takes about 10 of the 180 minutes. It is also the only group with no method marks to fall back on: an item is right or it is zero.

Practice items, not past questions

Every item below is an original practice item written to the CDC pattern. None is claimed to have appeared in a particular year's paper. Every numerical answer has been recomputed independently before it was written down.

17.1 Sequence and Series

Facts. For an arithmetic sequence, t_n=a+(n-1)d and S_n=\frac{n}{2}\{2a+(n-1)d\}. For a geometric sequence, t_n=ar^{n-1} and S_n=\frac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1} for r\ne1. The arithmetic mean of two numbers is \frac{a+b}{2}, the geometric mean is \sqrt{ab}, and for positive numbers AM \geq GM with equality only when the numbers are equal.

  1. The 10th term of the sequence 3, 7, 11, ... is [1]a35b39c40d43
  2. The number of terms in the sequence 5, 8, 11, ..., 47 is [1]a13b14c15d16
  3. Which term of the sequence 2, 5, 8, ... is 65? [1]a20thb21stc22ndd23rd
  4. The sum of the first 20 natural numbers is [1]a190b200c210d420
  5. The geometric mean of 4 and 9 is [1]a6b6.5c13d36
  6. If a and b are two unequal positive numbers, then [1]aAM > GMbAM < GMcAM = GMdAM = 2 GM
  7. The 5th term of the geometric sequence 3, 6, 12, ... is [1]a24b36c48d96
  8. The sum of 2 + 6 + 18 + ... + 1458 is [1]a2186b2187c1458d729
Answers to 17.1

1. (b) — a=3, d=4, t_{10}=3+9\times4=39.

2. (c) — 47=5+(n-1)3, so n-1=14 and n=15.

3. (c) — 65=2+(n-1)3, so n-1=21 and n=22.

4. (c) — S_{20}=\frac{20\times21}{2}=210.

5. (a) — \sqrt{4\times9}=\sqrt{36}=6.

6. (a) — (\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{b})^2>0 gives \frac{a+b}{2}>\sqrt{ab}.

7. (c) — t_5=3\times2^{4}=48.

8. (a) — the last term is 2\times3^{6}, so S_7=\frac{2(3^7-1)}{3-1}=2186.

17.2 Quadratic Equations and Graphs

Facts. For ax^2+bx+c=0 the roots are \frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}; the discriminant D=b^2-4ac decides the nature (real and unequal for D>0, equal for D=0, imaginary for D<0); the sum of the roots is -\frac{b}{a} and the product is \frac{c}{a}. The graph of y=ax^2+bx+c is a parabola opening up when a>0, and its vertex is at x=-\frac{b}{2a}.

  1. The discriminant of 2x^2-5x+3=0 is [1]a1b−1c49d25
  2. The roots of x^2-5x+6=0 are [1]a1, 6b2, 3c−2, −3d−1, −6
  3. If the roots of x^2+kx+9=0 are equal, then k is [1]a3b6c9d81
  4. The sum and the product of the roots of 3x^2-7x+2=0 are [1]a\frac{7}{3} and \frac{2}{3}b-\frac{7}{3} and \frac{2}{3}c\frac{7}{3} and -\frac{2}{3}d\frac{3}{7} and \frac{3}{2}
  5. The graph of y=x^2-4x+3 cuts the x-axis at [1]ax=1 and x=3bx=-1 and x=-3cx=0 and x=4dx=2 only
  6. The line of symmetry of the parabola y=x^2-6x+5 is [1]ax=3bx=-3cx=6dy=3
  7. If one root of x^2-7x+c=0 is 2, then c is [1]a2b5c10d14
  8. The roots of x^2+4=0 are [1]areal and equalbreal and unequalcimaginarydzero
Answers to 17.2

1. (a) — 25-4\times2\times3=25-24=1.

2. (b) — x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3).

3. (b) — equal roots need k^2=4\times9=36, so k=\pm6; of the options, 6.

4. (a) — sum =-\frac{b}{a}=\frac{7}{3}, product =\frac{c}{a}=\frac{2}{3}.

5. (a) — x^2-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3), so y=0 at x=1 and x=3.

6. (a) — x=-\frac{b}{2a}=\frac{6}{2}=3.

7. (c) — 2 is a root, so 4-14+c=0 and c=10.

8. (c) — D=0-16=-16<0, so the roots are imaginary (x=\pm2i).

17.3 Matrices and Determinants

Facts. A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m\times n; two matrices can be added only when their orders match, and multiplied only when the columns of the first equal the rows of the second. For a square matrix of order 2 with rows (a,b) and (c,d), the determinant is ad-bc — the leading diagonal product minus the other one — and the inverse \frac{1}{ad-bc} times the matrix with rows (d,-b) and (-c,a) exists only when ad-bc\ne0.

  1. The order of the matrix with 3 rows and 4 columns is [1]a3\times3b4\times4c3\times4d4\times3
  2. The determinant of the matrix with first row 5, 2 and second row 3, 4 is [1]a26b14c20d6
  3. A square matrix has an inverse only when its determinant is [1]azerobnot zerocpositivedone
  4. If A has order 2\times3 and B has order 3\times4, then AB has order [1]a2\times4b4\times2c3\times3dnot defined
  5. The value of x if the determinant with first row x, 3 and second row 4, 6 equals 12 is [1]a2b4c6d8
  6. The determinant of the identity matrix of order 3 is [1]a0b1c3d9
  7. Which of these matrices is singular? [1]afirst row 2, 1, second row 4, 3bfirst row 3, 6, second row 1, 2cfirst row 1, 0, second row 0, 1dfirst row 5, 2, second row 1, 4
  8. In Cramer's rule the value of y is [1]a\frac{D_y}{D}b\frac{D}{D_y}cD_yDd\frac{D_x}{D}
Answers to 17.3

1. (c) — rows first, then columns: 3\times4.

2. (b) — 5\times4-2\times3=20-6=14.

3. (b) — division by the determinant is impossible when it is zero.

4. (a) — the inner orders (3 and 3) cancel, leaving 2\times4.

5. (b) — 6x-12=12 gives 6x=24 and x=4.

6. (b) — every identity matrix has determinant 1.

7. (b) — 3\times2-6\times1=0.

8. (a) — y=\frac{D_y}{D} when D\ne0.

When the unknown is inside the matrix

An item of this shape asks for the letter in the matrix, not for the determinant, and the two numbers are usually different. Item 5 is the model: the determinant is given as 12 and the letter comes out as 4. Read which one the question wants, then substitute your answer back — 6(4)-12=12 — before you mark the option.

17.4 Trigonometry: Multiple, Submultiple and Transformation Formulas

Facts. \sin2A=2\sin A\cos A; \cos2A=\cos^2A-\sin^2A=1-2\sin^2A=2\cos^2A-1; \tan2A=\frac{2\tan A}{1-\tan^2A}; \sin3A=3\sin A-4\sin^3A; \cos3A=4\cos^3A-3\cos A; for submultiples \sin A=\frac{2\tan\frac{A}{2}}{1+\tan^2\frac{A}{2}} and \cos A=\frac{1-\tan^2\frac{A}{2}}{1+\tan^2\frac{A}{2}}; and the transformation formulas \sin C+\sin D=2\sin\frac{C+D}{2}\cos\frac{C-D}{2}, \sin C-\sin D=2\cos\frac{C+D}{2}\sin\frac{C-D}{2}, \cos C+\cos D=2\cos\frac{C+D}{2}\cos\frac{C-D}{2}, \cos C-\cos D=-2\sin\frac{C+D}{2}\sin\frac{C-D}{2}.

  1. If \sin A=\frac{3}{5} and A is acute, then \sin2A is [1]a\frac{6}{5}b\frac{24}{25}c\frac{7}{25}d\frac{12}{25}
  2. The value of 2\sin15°\cos15° is [1]a\frac{1}{2}b\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}c1d\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}
  3. \cos2A in terms of \sin A alone is [1]a1+2\sin^2Ab1-2\sin^2Ac2\sin^2A-1d2\sin A\cos A
  4. If \tan A=\frac{1}{2}, then \tan2A is [1]a\frac{3}{4}b\frac{4}{3}c1d\frac{1}{4}
  5. \sin3A equals [1]a3\sin A-4\sin^3Ab4\sin^3A-3\sin Ac3\sin A+4\sin^3Ad3\sin^3A
  6. \sin40°+\sin20° equals [1]a\sin60°b2\sin30°\cos10°c\cos30°d2\cos30°\cos10°
  7. \cos40°-\cos20° equals [1]a-2\sin30°\sin10°b2\sin30°\sin10°c-2\cos30°\cos10°d2\cos30°\sin10°
  8. The value of \frac{\sin2A}{1+\cos2A} is [1]a\tan Ab\cot Ac\tan2Ad\sec A
  9. \cos^2A-\sin^2A equals [1]a2\sin Ab\cos2Ac\sin2Ad1
  10. If \sin A=\cos A and A is acute, then 2A is [1]a45°b60°c90°d180°
Answers to 17.4

1. (b) — \cos A=\frac{4}{5}, so \sin2A=2\times\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{4}{5}=\frac{24}{25}.

2. (a) — 2\sin15°\cos15°=\sin30°=\frac{1}{2}.

3. (b) — from the three forms of \cos2A, the one with only \sin A is 1-2\sin^2A.

4. (b) — \tan2A=\frac{2\times\frac{1}{2}}{1-\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{1}{\frac{3}{4}}=\frac{4}{3}.

5. (a) — the standard identity; (b) is -\sin3A.

6. (b) — 2\sin30°\cos10°, which is about 0.98, the value of \sin40°+\sin20°.

7. (a) — the minus form carries the negative sign: -2\sin30°\sin10°\approx-0.174.

8. (a) — \frac{2\sin A\cos A}{2\cos^2A}=\tan A.

9. (b) — that is the definition of \cos2A.

10. (c) — A=45°, so 2A=90°.

17.5 Conditional Identities, Trigonometric Equations and Height and Distance

Facts. Three conditional identities govern most items of this type: in a triangle, \sin2A+\sin2B+\sin2C=4\sin A\sin B\sin C, \cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C=1-2\cos A\cos B\cos C and \tan A+\tan B+\tan C=\tan A\tan B\tan C. A trigonometric equation is solved by reducing it to a single ratio and writing the general value of the angle.

  1. In any triangle, \sin2A+\sin2B+\sin2C equals [1]a4\cos A\cos B\cos Cb4\sin A\sin B\sin Cc0d2\sin A\sin B\sin C
  2. If A+B+C=180°, then \tan A+\tan B+\tan C equals [1]a\tan A\tan B\tan Cb0c1d\cot A\cot B\cot C
  3. If \sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} and 0°\leq\theta\leq90°, then \theta is [1]a30°b45°c60°d90°
  4. The general solution of \tan\theta=1 is [1]an\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}b2n\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}cn\pi-\frac{\pi}{4}d\frac{n\pi}{2}
  5. A pole 10 m high casts a shadow 10 m long. The elevation of the sun is [1]a30°b45°c60°d90°
  6. From a point 20 m from the foot of a tower the angle of elevation of the top is 45°. The height of the tower is [1]a10 mb20 mc20\sqrt{3} md40 m
  7. The angle of depression is measured [1]aupward from the horizontalbdownward from the horizontalcfrom the verticaldalong the ground
  8. If \cos\theta=\frac{1}{2} and \theta is acute, then \theta is [1]a30°b45°c60°d120°
Answers to 17.5

1. (b) — \sin2A+\sin2B+\sin2C=4\sin A\sin B\sin C in a triangle.

2. (a) — the tangent identity for a triangle sum: they are equal.

3. (c) — \sin60°=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.

4. (a) — tangent has period \pi, so \theta=n\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}.

5. (b) — \tan\theta=\frac{10}{10}=1, so the elevation is 45°.

6. (b) — \tan45°=1, so height = distance =20 m.

7. (b) — the depression is the angle below the horizontal.

8. (c) — \cos60°=\frac{1}{2}; 120° has the same cosine but is obtuse.

17.6 Angle between Two Lines and Pair of Straight Lines

Facts. If two lines of slopes m_1 and m_2 meet at an angle \theta, then \tan\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|. The lines are parallel when m_1=m_2 and perpendicular when m_1m_2=-1. A homogeneous equation of the second degree ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0 represents a pair of straight lines through the origin, and the angle between them satisfies \tan\theta=\left|\frac{2\sqrt{h^2-ab}}{a+b}\right|, the lines being perpendicular when a+b=0.

  1. The slope of the line 3x+4y=12 is [1]a\frac{3}{4}b-\frac{3}{4}c\frac{4}{3}d-\frac{4}{3}
  2. The lines 2x+3y=5 and 4x+6y=7 are [1]aperpendicularbparallelccoincidentdintersecting at 45°
  3. If two lines of slopes m_1 and m_2 are perpendicular, then [1]am_1=m_2bm_1m_2=1cm_1m_2=-1dm_1+m_2=0
  4. The angle between the lines y=x and y=\sqrt{3}x is [1]a15°b30°c45°d60°
  5. The equation x^2-y^2=0 represents [1]aa circleba pair of perpendicular linesca parabolada single line
  6. For the pair of lines ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0 to be perpendicular, we need [1]aa=bba=-bch^2=abdh=0
Answers to 17.6

1. (b) — rearranging gives y=-\frac{3}{4}x+3.

2. (b) — the second equation is the first multiplied by 2, with a different constant, so the slopes match and the lines never meet.

3. (c) — perpendicular slopes multiply to -1.

4. (a) — slopes 1 and \sqrt{3}, so \tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{1+\sqrt{3}}=2-\sqrt{3}\approx0.268, and \tan15°=2-\sqrt{3}, so \theta=15°.

5. (b) — x^2-y^2=(x-y)(x+y)=0 gives the lines y=x and y=-x.

6. (b) — a+b=0 is the perpendicular condition.

The two-minute habit that saves these marks

In item 4 the two slopes are 1 and 1.732, and the value 0.268 that comes out of the formula does not look like any angle on the page. The habit that never fails is: compute the number, then compare it with a value you already know. \tan15°\approx0.27 and \tan30°\approx0.58, so the angle is 15°. Carry that habit into every Group A item.

17.7 Conic Sections and Circle

Facts. The circle with centre (h,k) and radius r has equation (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2, and the general equation x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0 has centre (-g,-f) and radius \sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}. A parabola has eccentricity 1, an ellipse less than 1 and a hyperbola more than 1.

  1. The centre of the circle x^2+y^2-6x+4y-12=0 is [1]a(3,-2)b(-3,2)c(6,-4)d(3,2)
  2. The radius of the circle in item 1 is [1]a5b25c12d13
  3. The equation of the circle with centre (0,0) and radius 4 is [1]ax^2+y^2=2bx^2+y^2=4cx^2+y^2=8dx^2+y^2=16
  4. The eccentricity of a parabola is [1]a0bless than 1c1dmore than 1
  5. The conic with eccentricity greater than 1 is [1]acirclebellipsecparaboladhyperbola
  6. The distance of the point (3,4) from the origin is [1]a5b7c12d25
  7. If the circle x^2+y^2+4x+2y+c=0 passes through the origin, then c is [1]a0b4c2d−4
  8. The circle x^2+y^2+2x+2y+2=0 has [1]aradius 2bradius \sqrt{2}cno real circledradius 0
Answers to 17.7

1. (a) — compare with x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c: g=-3, f=2, centre (-g,-f)=(3,-2).

2. (a) — r=\sqrt{9+4+12}=\sqrt{25}=5.

3. (d) — radius squared is 16.

4. (c) — every point of a parabola is equidistant from the focus and the directrix, so e=1.

5. (d) — an eccentricity greater than 1 gives a hyperbola.

6. (a) — \sqrt{9+16}=5.

7. (a) — putting x=y=0 leaves c=0.

8. (c) — r^2=g^2+f^2-c=1+1-2=0, so the "circle" is a single point.

17.8 Vector

Facts. If \vec a=a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j and \vec b=b_1\hat i+b_2\hat j, then \vec a\cdot\vec b=a_1b_1+a_2b_2=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta; \vec a and \vec b are perpendicular when the dot product is zero and parallel when \frac{a_1}{b_1}=\frac{a_2}{b_2}. The magnitude of \vec a is \sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2}, and the position vector of the point dividing AB internally in the ratio m:n is \frac{m\vec b+n\vec a}{m+n}.

  1. If \vec a=2\hat i+3\hat j and \vec b=4\hat i-\hat j, then \vec a\cdot\vec b is [1]a5b11c8d−3
  2. The magnitude of \vec a=3\hat i+4\hat j is [1]a5b7c12d25
  3. The vectors 2\hat i+\hat j and x\hat i+2\hat j are perpendicular when x is [1]a1b−1c2d−2
  4. The unit vector along 3\hat i+4\hat j is [1]a3\hat i+4\hat jb\frac{3\hat i+4\hat j}{5}c\frac{3\hat i+4\hat j}{7}d5(3\hat i+4\hat j)
  5. If \vec a=2\hat i+\hat j and \vec b=4\hat i+2\hat j, the two vectors are [1]aparallelbperpendicularcequaldopposite
  6. The position vector of the midpoint of A(2,3) and B(4,7) is [1]a3\hat i+5\hat jb6\hat i+10\hat jc2\hat i+4\hat jd\hat i+2\hat j
  7. If \vec a\cdot\vec b=0 and neither vector is zero, the angle between them is [1]a0°b45°c90°d180°
  8. The value of |\hat i+\hat j| is [1]a1b\sqrt{2}c2d0
Answers to 17.8

1. (a) — 2\times4+3\times(-1)=8-3=5.

2. (a) — \sqrt{9+16}=5.

3. (b) — 2x+2=0 gives x=-1; check: 2(-1)+1(2)=0.

4. (b) — divide by the magnitude 5.

5. (a) — \vec b=2\vec a, so they are parallel.

6. (a) — the midpoint is (3,5).

7. (c) — \cos\theta=0, so \theta=90°.

8. (b) — \sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt{2}.

The substitution habit

Every item in this chapter that asks for a letter has a "near miss" option next to the right one, because that is how real papers are built. The cheap insurance is the same every time: find the value, then put it back into the condition the question stated. For item 3 that means checking that 2(-1)+1(2) really is zero before you darken the bubble.

17.9 Linear Programming and Transformation

Facts. A linear programming problem has an objective function to be maximised or minimised, constraints written as linear inequalities, and a feasible region that is always convex. The best value is attained at a corner of that region. A transformation with matrix rows (a,b) and (c,d) sends the point (x,y) to (ax+by,\;cx+dy); an inversion transformation with centre O and radius k sends P to P' on the same ray with OP\cdot OP'=k^2.

  1. In linear programming the objective function is [1]aa constraintbthe quantity to be maximised or minimisedcthe feasible regionda corner point
  2. The maximum of a linear objective over a feasible region is attained [1]aat the centrebat a corner pointcanywheredoutside the region
  3. The point (2,3) under the identity transformation goes to [1]a(3,2)b(2,3)c(-2,-3)d(0,0)
  4. Under the transformation with matrix first row 0, −1 and second row 1, 0, the point (3,4) goes to [1]a(-4,3)b(4,-3)c(3,-4)d(-3,4)
  5. In an inversion transformation with radius k, the product OP\cdot OP' equals [1]akbk^2c2kd1
  6. The region satisfying x\geq0, y\geq0 and x+y\leq4 is [1]aa triangleba squarecunboundedda single point
  7. The maximum of z=x+y subject to x\geq0, y\geq0, x+y\leq4 is [1]a0b2c4d8
  8. A point on the inversion circle is [1]amoved onto itselfbsent to the centrecsent to infinitydlost
Answers to 17.9

1. (b) — the objective is what the problem asks you to maximise or minimise.

2. (b) — a linear function on a convex polygon peaks at a vertex.

3. (b) — the identity matrix leaves every point fixed.

4. (a) — (0\times3+(-1)\times4,\;1\times3+0\times4)=(-4,3).

5. (b) — that product is the defining property, OP\cdot OP'=k^2.

6. (a) — the three lines close a right triangle with corners (0,0), (4,0), (0,4).

7. (c) — z is largest at (4,0) or (0,4), where z=4.

8. (a) — a point at distance k from the centre satisfies OP\cdot OP'=k^2 with OP'=k, so it is its own image.

17.10 Continuity

Facts. A function is continuous at x=a when the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and the value of the function at a are all the same number. If the two one-sided limits differ, the gap is a jump discontinuity; if the limit exists but f(a) is different, the point is a removable discontinuity.

  1. A function f is continuous at x=a if [1]af(a) existsbthe limit existscthe limit exists and equals f(a)df is increasing
  2. The value of \lim_{x\to2}(3x+1) is [1]a5b6c7ddoes not exist
  3. The value of \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x} is [1]a0b1c\inftyddoes not exist
  4. The function f(x)=\frac{1}{x} is discontinuous at [1]ax=0bx=1cevery xdno point
  5. If \lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=3 and \lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=5, then at a the function has [1]aa removable discontinuityba jump discontinuitycno discontinuityda maximum
  6. The value of \lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^2-9}{x-3} is [1]a0b3c6ddoes not exist
Answers to 17.10

1. (c) — continuity needs the limit and the value to agree.

2. (c) — 3\times2+1=7, and a polynomial is continuous everywhere.

3. (b) — the standard limit is 1.

4. (a) — at x=0 the expression is undefined and grows without bound.

5. (b) — the one-sided limits differ, which is a jump.

6. (c) — cancel the factor: \frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}=x+3\to6.

17.11 Statistics: Measures of Dispersion

Facts. For a set of n observations with mean \bar x, the mean deviation about the mean is \frac{\sum|x-\bar x|}{n}; the standard deviation is \sigma=\sqrt{\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n}}, the variance is \sigma^2, and the coefficient of variation is \frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100\%. The quartile deviation is \frac{Q_3-Q_1}{2}.

  1. The range of 4, 9, 2, 7, 11 is [1]a7b9c11d5
  2. The mean of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is [1]a5b6c7d30
  3. The standard deviation of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is [1]a\sqrt{8}b8c\sqrt{40}d2
  4. If every observation is increased by 5, the standard deviation [1]aincreases by 5bis unchangedcis multiplied by 5ddoubles
  5. The coefficient of variation is a measure of [1]acentral tendencybrelative dispersionccorrelationdskewness
  6. If Q_1=20 and Q_3=40, the quartile deviation is [1]a10b20c30d60
  7. For a distribution with mean 50 and standard deviation 5, the coefficient of variation is [1]a5%b10%c25%d50%
  8. The standard deviation of a set in which every observation is equal is [1]aequal to the observationb1c0dundefined
Answers to 17.11

17.12 Functions and Polynomials

Facts. A relation is a set of ordered pairs; a function sends each input to exactly one output, which the vertical line test checks on a graph. For f(x)=ax^2+bx+c the remainder on division by x-a is f(a) (remainder theorem), and x-a is a factor exactly when f(a)=0 (factor theorem). Chapter summary

  • Sequences: t_n=a+(n-1)d, S_n=\frac n2\{2a+(n-1)d\}, t_n=ar^{n-1}, S_n=\frac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}; AM =\frac{a+b}{2}, GM =\sqrt{ab}, and AM \geq GM.
  • Quadratic: D=b^2-4ac fixes the nature of the roots; sum of roots =-\frac ba, product =\frac ca; vertex at x=-\frac{b}{2a}.
  • Matrices: order is rows \times columns; a square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is not zero.
  • Trigonometry: know \sin2A, the three forms of \cos2A, \tan2A, \sin3A, \cos3A, the four transformation formulas, and the four half-angle results.
  • Conditional identities: in a triangle, \tan A+\tan B+\tan C=\tan A\tan B\tan C and \sin2A+\sin2B+\sin2C=4\sin A\sin B\sin C.
  • Lines: \tan\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|; parallel means equal slopes, perpendicular means the slopes multiply to -1.
  • Circle: centre (-g,-f) and radius \sqrt{g^2+f^2-c} for x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0.
  • Vectors: \vec a\cdot\vec b=a_1b_1+a_2b_2; zero dot product means perpendicular.
  • Dispersion: \sigma=\sqrt{\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n}}, CV =\frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100\%, quartile deviation =\frac{Q_3-Q_1}{2}.
  • Polynomials: remainder =f(a) on division by x-a; x-a is a factor exactly when f(a)=0.
